title: KV compressology: multi-precision allocator experiment and fidelity rollback playbook
creator: Liam O'Connor
description: Evaluate a layered, request-aware KV compression strategy ("compressology") that dynamically allocates precision per token-cohort and per-prefix to minimize GPU memory while preserving generation quality. The core idea is an allocator that assigns FP8/INT8/INT4 encodings to KV shards based on recent access frequency, prefix length, and a lightweight fidelity score; when fidelity drops below thresholds, the runtime transparently upgrades shards (rollback) for affected cohorts. This ticket covers experiment design, infra to collect fidelity signals, controlled runs on internal traffic, measurement of QoR regressions, and a playbook for automated rollback triggers and canary rollout to production.
acceptance_criteria: End-to-end experiment pipeline that runs compressology policy variants across three models (redwood-small, redwood-medium, redwood-large) on synthetic and sampled real traffic
Quantified quality trade-offs: per-cohort delta in generation metrics (perplexity, ROUGE-L, response-fidelity) with 95% CI
Memory reduction and throughput numbers (GPU memory peak, tokens/sec) for each precision mix (FP8-only, FP8+INT8 hybrid, tiered-int4 fallback)
A documented rollback/playbook with concrete thresholds, alerting dashboard, and a staging canary runbook
A PR with runtime hooks for per-shard precision metadata and a flag for enforced rollback available for canary testing
steps: Define cohorting rules and fidelity score (attention heat + token novelty + response divergence)
Implement per-shard precision metadata and allocator simulation in local runtime branch
Build an eval harness: sample prompts (1k curated + 20k random) and baseline runs (no compression)
Run batch experiments across model sizes with traffic replay at 1x and 5x traffic intensity
Collect metrics to dashboards and artifact storage (S3) and run statistical comparisons
Iterate on thresholds and policies, implement automated rollback hook in runtime
Draft playbook and prepare staging canary with monitoring and alerting rules
Open PRs, solicit PM/Design/Infra review, and schedule runtime canary window
experiment_design: We test a policy family where each KV shard is scored every N tokens. Score combines: access frequency (t-decayed), prefix-criticality (long prefixes weighted higher), and fidelity slack (recent perplexity drift). Candidate encodings: FP8 (baseline high-fidelity low-memory), INT8 (moderate), INT4 (aggressive). The allocator maps shards to encodings subject to a global GPU-memory budget. Two runtime variants: (A) warm-up-only allocator that only compacts cold shards, (B) aggressive allocator that compacts by cohort and allows asynchronous rollback if fidelity delta > threshold. We run each policy with and without KV-prefetch caching to observe interaction with continuous batching. Key knobs: score window (50/200 tokens), rollback threshold (delta perplexity 0.5/1.0/2.0), compaction frequency (per-request vs. batch-window).
datasets: synthetic/zipf-skewed-10k (to stress tiering and cohort skew)
metrics: generation ROUGE-L and exact-match for structured outputs
GPU memory peak and memory reduction percentage
rollback rate (rollbacks per 1k requests) and time-to-rollback
fraction of tokens served from compacted shards (cache hit-like metric)
hypothesis: A smart, cohort-aware allocator that uses FP8 for hot/high-fidelity shards and INT8/INT4 for cold or low-fidelity shards can reduce GPU working set by 30-55% with <1.5% relative degradation in primary generation metrics for the median cohort. Aggressive INT4 on long-tail cold shards will show larger quality regressions on rare, high-fidelity prompts and thus requires conservative rollback thresholds or fallbacks during canary.
results_summary: Preliminary runs (redwood-small, 1k prompt subset) show ~38% GPU memory reduction with a hybrid FP8+INT8 policy and median perplexity delta of +0.9%. The INT4-tiered variant reached 52% reduction but produced top-decile cohort regressions (perplexity deltas up to +6.5%) on long-context math/programming prompts. Rollback triggers fired correctly in the simulation branch and average time-to-rollback measured ~120ms in the local emulation; in-situ wall-clock may be higher once integrated into continuous batching. Next: scale to redwood-medium, add traffic skew tests, and tighten rollback latency to <=50ms for production canary.
risks: Long-tail quality regressions impacting SLAs for enterprise customers
KV fragmentation leading to inefficient memory usage and higher allocation churn
Rollback latency too high under heavy batching, causing visible errors before recovery
Complexity of per-shard metadata increases allocation overhead and may regress throughput
False positive rollbacks causing unnecessary storage churn
